title: Choosing a way and a method

blocks.heading: Choosing a way and a method
blocks.text: Verbal communication uses spoken words, written communication uses text and visual communication uses images, symbols or graphical displays. Letters and meetings are methods, while these ways describe how meaning is expressed. A meeting can combine spoken discussion, written handouts and a visual diagram. Verbal discussion can give fast clarification and personal contact, but may leave no reliable record unless recorded appropriately. Written text provides something to consult and can specify details, but the receiver must access and understand it; replies may not be immediate. Visuals can make a layout or trend clearer, but unfamiliar symbols or missing labels can mislead. Choose using urgency, audience access and language, complexity, confidentiality, cost and the need for feedback or proof. Combining methods can be more suitable than claiming one is best for every message.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Uda Repairs must explain a new machine layout to workers and retain the agreed operating instructions. A spoken demonstration with a labelled layout can clarify positions and allow questions; a concise written instruction provides a later reference. An unlabelled picture or a long letter alone may not resolve practical misunderstandings.

blocks.heading: Verbal communication
blocks.text: Verbal communication uses spoken words, for example conversation, a telephone call or a spoken presentation. It can suit urgent clarification and sensitive discussion where tone helps meaning. Without a retained record, details may be forgotten or disputed. Noise, unfamiliar terms or not allowing questions can make spoken communication ineffective.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Veya Repairs phones a customer to clarify an unusual repair request. The call can resolve questions quickly. The final agreed work and price should be confirmed in a suitable record if needed, rather than assuming memory will preserve every detail.

blocks.heading: Written communication
blocks.text: Written communication conveys meaning through text, such as letters, emails, instructions or reports. It can preserve details for later reference and reach people who cannot meet at once. It depends on access and reading comprehension and may delay clarification. A written record demonstrates the content supplied, but not automatically that every intended person read or understood it.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ema Clothing sends detailed order specifications by an accessible email. The specifications can be consulted during production. Confirming the supplier’s understanding helps prevent an unnoticed ambiguity from becoming an incorrect order.

blocks.heading: Visual communication
blocks.text: Visual communication conveys information through images, symbols, diagrams, charts or other graphical representations. It can make spatial layouts or patterns easier to understand than a long verbal description. Clear labels, an appropriate scale and audience familiarity matter; a symbol that nobody recognises does not communicate effectively. Visuals often work best with a short explanation.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tola Stores uses a labelled floor plan to show where stock should be placed. The plan can make the required location clear. Missing labels or an unclear orientation would limit its usefulness even if the drawing looks attractive.

blocks.heading: Letters
blocks.text: A business letter is a written message addressed to a particular recipient, commonly used for formal detailed communication. It can provide a record, explain terms and present information in an organised form. Delivery and response can take time, and the reader must understand the wording. Choose an appropriately secure and timely delivery method instead of assuming a letter suits an immediate emergency.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Owa Supply writes to a customer confirming agreed delivery terms. A retained letter can record the agreement. It is less suitable as the sole method for an urgent change if the customer will receive it after dispatch.

blocks.heading: Meetings
blocks.text: A meeting brings participants together, physically or through a suitable communication channel, to share information, discuss issues or make decisions. It can allow questions and draw on several perspectives, but consumes time and may be dominated by a few voices. An agenda can focus the discussion and minutes can record decisions, responsibilities and deadlines. Holding a meeting does not itself ensure everyone understands or agrees.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Iha Foods brings production and sales staff together to coordinate a major order. The meeting can resolve conflicting promises through immediate discussion. Recording the agreed quantity, date and responsible people helps prevent different memories afterwards.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Communication and a context-dependent choice
blocks.text:
Tuli Stores must explain a complex revised rota and hear staff concerns before it starts next week. All affected workers can attend a quiet meeting tomorrow, and a printed summary can record final arrangements. Email access is uneven. For part (b) only, workers are now dispersed across locations and cannot attend one meeting before the deadline, but all have reliable phone access. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Tuli’s meeting and summary under the original facts, compared with email alone. [12]
b Evaluate how the method should change when staff are dispersed but all have reliable phone access. Explain which communication needs remain. [12]

a A quiet meeting suits a complex change needing staff concerns and immediate clarification. All can attend before implementation, while email access is uneven. A summary preserves the final rota and responsibilities. Manage the meeting so quieter staff can ask questions; attendance alone does not prove understanding. Prefer this combination because it addresses access, complexity and feedback. b A single meeting no longer reaches everyone in time, so the original attendance condition fails. Use scheduled phone discussions or a suitable phone conference to explain the changes and hear responses, then provide each worker with an accessible record of their final rota. Reliable phone access supports verbal contact but does not imply reliable email, so confirm how the written record will reach each worker. Exact timing, opportunity for feedback and understanding checks remain essential. The channel changes because access changes, while the purpose and need for a record remain.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Communication and a context-dependent choice
blocks.text:
Omu Workshop must tell workers that tomorrow’s shift begins one hour earlier. Everyone is present today, but machinery is noisy and some workers have no email access. A supervisor suggests a quiet spoken briefing with questions plus a clearly dated printed reminder. Another manager suggests email alone.

a Explain how Omu’s proposed approach addresses access, noise and misunderstanding. [8]
b Evaluate whether using both verbal and written communication is justified for this simple but urgent message. [12]

a Moving away from machinery reduces interference with the spoken message. Briefing staff while everyone is present reaches those without email. The supervisor should give the exact date and time, invite questions and ask staff to confirm the arrangement, exposing any mistaken interpretation. The printed reminder provides a reference after the briefing. A clear reminder alone would not necessarily identify who had misunderstood; verbal contact alone could leave forgotten details. Together the channels address distinct barriers. b The content is simple, so a large formal meeting would be excessive. A short quiet briefing with a concise reminder is proportionate because the change is urgent, all staff are currently reachable and uneven email access makes email alone unreliable. The combination uses some staff time and printing, but avoids a missed shift start and provides both clarification and a retained record of the new start time. Choose the concise combination and confirm any absent person separately. If every worker had reliable access and acknowledged a clear written update, the extra briefing might be less necessary; that is not the current case.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Communication and a context-dependent choice
blocks.text:
Omu Workshop must tell workers that tomorrow’s shift begins one hour earlier. Everyone is present today, but machinery is noisy and some workers have no email access. A supervisor suggests a quiet spoken briefing with questions plus a clearly dated printed reminder. Another manager suggests email alone.

a(i) Define effective communication. [2]
a(ii) State two barriers shown at Omu. [2]
b State two reasons a business needs effective communication. [2]
c Explain why the proposed briefing and reminder suit Omu’s change. [6]
d Evaluate email alone against the proposed combined method. [8]

a(i) The intended message reaches the intended receiver and is understood as intended. a(ii) Machine noise and lack of email access for some workers. b Coordinating work and preventing misunderstandings in instructions. c A quiet briefing avoids the stated noise and allows immediate questions, while everyone is present. A dated written reminder preserves the exact start time for later consultation. Checking staff can repeat the arrangement helps establish understanding rather than merely transmission. d Email can provide a written record and reach accessible accounts quickly, but it excludes workers without access and may not be read before tomorrow. Use the quiet briefing plus reminder, with understanding checked. Email can supplement for those who use it, but is insufficient as the sole channel under the stated facts. The method is chosen for access, timing and feedback, not because spoken communication is universally superior.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Communication and a context-dependent choice
blocks.text:
Tuli Stores must explain a complex revised rota and hear staff concerns before it starts next week. All affected workers can attend a quiet meeting tomorrow, and a printed summary can record final arrangements. Email access is uneven.

Evaluate a quiet meeting with a printed summary against email alone for Tuli. Give a concise plan. [12]

Purpose: understanding a complex rota and hearing concerns before next week. Meeting benefit: all affected workers can attend, discuss ambiguities and give feedback; quiet conditions reduce noise. Printed summary: records the final date, times and responsibilities after discussion. Limitations: meeting time and possible unequal participation need an agenda and opportunities to speak. Email alone: provides text and a record but uneven access risks excluding workers and responses may be late. Judgement: choose the meeting plus accessible summary; confirm understanding rather than assuming attendance proves it. Reconsider the delivery method if common attendance becomes impossible.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why “sender and feedback” does not answer a request for two ways of communication. Kena Goods uses a spoken briefing and a written reminder for a rota change.

Sender and feedback are elements of the communication process: who originates the message and the response. Spoken or verbal and written are ways in which the message is expressed. Internal/external is another classification about the business boundary. In Kena’s case the briefing is verbal and the reminder written; naming process elements would not identify those ways.
